The Five Great Lakes. The largest system of fresh water by surface area on Earth straddles the border between the United States and Canada. Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario are interconnected lakes shaped by glaciation and have defined North American geography, commerce, and ecology for millennia. Together they hold roughly twenty percent of the world's surface fresh water and remain vital to shipping, industry, and settlement in the Great Lakes region.

Superior is the largest by surface area at thirty-one thousand seven hundred square miles, the deepest, and the coldest, bordering Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Ontario. Michigan is the only Great Lake wholly within the United States, bordered by Michigan, Indiana, Illinois, and Wisconsin. Huron is the second-largest by surface area and lies between Michigan and Ontario, connected to Superior via the Saint Marys River. Erie is the shallowest and warms fastest, connecting the upper lakes through Niagara Falls and the Welland Canal to Ontario and the Saint Lawrence River. Ontario is the smallest by surface area but second-deepest, lying between New York and Ontario and draining eastward into the Saint Lawrence toward the Atlantic.

The lakes are connected by natural straits and engineering works, especially the Welland Canal, which bypasses Niagara Falls, forming a single navigable system. They were carved by glacial retreat at the end of the last ice age and fed by drainage from melting glaciers across the continent.
